Subclipse (and SVN tooling in general) has no built-in "commit on save" hook, because Eclipse's save action only touches the local file, not the SVN working copy — Subclipse never watches for saves. The practical fix is to build this yourself outside Eclipse: run a lightweight file-system watcher script (e.g. Python's `watchdog` library) that fires `svn commit -m "auto"` whenever a file under the working copy changes:

```python
from watchdog.observers import Observer
from watchdog.events import FileSystemEventHandler
import subprocess

class H(FileSystemEventHandler):
    def on_modified(self, event):
        subprocess.run(["svn", "commit", "-m", "auto-save"], cwd="path/to/wc")

Observer().schedule(H(), "path/to/wc", recursive=True)
```
Note this is generally risky for SVN: commits without meaningful messages pollute history and can commit half-finished code. Consider committing manually, or rely on Eclipse's Local History (already automatic) for the "undo to any save" use case instead.

`spreadsheets().values()` methods address ranges by sheet *name*, not by `gid` — that's why your append only ever hits the sheet named in the range string. To write to other sheets in the same spreadsheet, first look up their titles via `spreadsheets().get()`, then prefix the range with that title:

```python
meta = sheet.get(spreadsheetId=SAMPLE_SPREADSHEET_ID).execute()
for s in meta['sheets']:
    print(s['properties']['sheetId'], s['properties']['title'])

def UPDATE_GSHEET(sheet_name, some_data, cell_range="A1:W1"):
    body = {"majorDimension": "ROWS", "values": some_data}
    sheet.values().update(
        spreadsheetId=SAMPLE_SPREADSHEET_ID,
        range=f"{sheet_name}!{cell_range}",
        valueInputOption="USER_ENTERED",
        body=body
    ).execute()
```
If you only have the gid, map it to the title from the `get()` call above — the Sheets API's `values()` endpoints accept A1-notation ranges with the sheet name, never the gid directly.

The bug is `newlist=[oglist.split(',')]` — wrapping the split result in `[...]` makes `newlist` a list containing exactly one element: the full list of names. So `random.choice(newlist)` has only one possible choice (that one inner list) and "randomly" picks it every time, printing the whole list `num` times. Drop the extra brackets:

```python
def listgen(num):
    newlist = oglist.split(',')
    for x in range(num):
        print(random.choice(newlist))
```
Now `newlist` is a flat list of names, so `random.choice` picks a single name each call. Optionally strip whitespace since your split output has leading spaces (`' Frank'`): `newlist = [n.strip() for n in oglist.split(',')]`.

This is expected CPython behavior, not a bug. `id()` only guarantees uniqueness for objects alive at the same time; it says nothing about objects that no longer exist. Each call to `add_item()` creates a new list (`list_x = list_x + [3]`) local to that call. Once the function returns, nothing references that list, so CPython's reference-counting GC frees the memory immediately. A later call can then allocate a new object at that same now-free address, so `id()` returns the same value even though it's a different object with a non-overlapping lifetime.

To confirm, keep references alive:
```python
a = add_item()
b = add_item([1, 2])
c = add_item()
print(id(a) == id(c))  # False now, since a is still referenced
```
`id()` reuse across non-overlapping lifetimes is normal and harmless — it only becomes a bug if you rely on `id()` to distinguish objects whose lifetimes you haven't verified overlap.

Track a stack of people currently IN, in timestamp order; each OUT pops the matching name, and the next person to leave is whoever remains on top of the stack (the most recent still-pending IN).

```python
import pandas as pd

def last_in_first_out(path):
    df = pd.read_csv(path, parse_dates=['Time']).sort_values('Time')
    stack = []
    for _, row in df.iterrows():
        if row['Event'] == 'IN':
            stack.append(row['Executed'])
        else:  # OUT
            if stack and stack[-1] == row['Executed']:
                stack.pop()
            else:
                stack.remove(row['Executed'])
    return stack[-1] if stack else None
```
Processing your example leaves `stack == ['Kenny', 'Kyle']`, so `stack[-1]` returns `'Kyle'`, matching your expected result; after Kyle actually leaves, the next call would return `'Kenny'`.

This is a known FastAPI/Pydantic-v2 quirk: when a Pydantic model is bound to query params via `Annotated[Model, Query()]`, FastAPI validates the raw query strings in a stricter mode, so `"10"` never gets coerced to the int `10` before hitting `Literal[5, 10, 15]` — `Literal` does exact-type matching, and a string never satisfies an int literal.

Fixes, pick one:
1. Widen the Literal to accept both forms:
```python
number_of_questions: Union[Literal[5, 10, 15, "5", "10", "15"], None] = None
```
2. Add a `field_validator` that casts to int before the literal check:
```python
@field_validator("number_of_questions", mode="before")
def to_int(cls, v):
    return int(v) if v is not None else v
```
3. Stop binding via a model for this field and declare it as a plain function parameter (`number_of_questions: Literal[5,10,15] = Query(None)`), where FastAPI's normal query coercion applies correctly.

`sys.argv` is a single global list owned by the running process, not something tied to whichever module you're in — when A imports B, `sys.argv` is still whatever A was launched with, so code in B reading `sys.argv` at import time gets wrong values or crashes.

The real fix is to stop having B read `sys.argv` directly at module level. Refactor B so its logic lives in a function taking explicit parameters, guarded by `if __name__ == '__main__':`:

```python
# B.py
def run(x, y):
    ...

if __name__ == '__main__':
    import sys
    run(int(sys.argv[1]), int(sys.argv[2]))
```
```python
# A.py
import B
B.run(30, 10)
```
If you can't edit B, you can set `sys.argv = ['B.py', '30', '10']` before `import B`, but that's fragile and affects the whole process's argv state.

Django's built-in auth views (`LoginView`, etc.) reference `registration/login.html` but ship no such template themselves — the book expects you to create it. Your traceback shows Django only checked `django/contrib/admin/templates/registration/`, meaning it never reached your app's own template directory.

Fix:
1. Create `your_app/templates/registration/login.html` — the `registration` subfolder name is hardcoded by Django's auth views, so it must match exactly.
2. Confirm the app containing that `templates/` folder is listed in `INSTALLED_APPS`.
3. Confirm `TEMPLATES[0]['APP_DIRS']` is `True` in settings.py, so Django's app-directories loader searches each app's `templates/` folder automatically.
4. Give the template minimal content extending your base template, with `{% csrf_token %}` and `{{ form.as_p }}`.

Also set `LOGIN_REDIRECT_URL` in settings, otherwise you'll hit a follow-up error immediately after a successful login.

Python decides at compile time whether a name is local to a function: if there's *any* assignment to that name anywhere in the function body (including `b += 1`, which is `b = b + 1`), Python treats `b` as local for the whole function, even before that line executes. So inside `B()`, `b` is local, and `b += 1` tries to read it before it has a local value, raising `UnboundLocalError`. Your second example only *reads* `b` and never assigns to it, so Python resolves it as a free variable from the enclosing scope via the closure, which works fine.

To update the outer `b` from inside `B`, declare it explicitly:
```python
def A():
    b = 1
    def B():
        nonlocal b
        b += 1
        return b
    return B()
```
`nonlocal` tells Python that assignments to `b` inside `B` should target the enclosing scope's variable instead of creating a new local one.

`for i in newString: slicedString = myList[2:-2]` loops over individual *characters* of `newString` (`i` is never used) and reassigns `slicedString` to a slice of the whole `myList` every iteration — that's why only the first/last two characters of the entire blob get trimmed, not each record.

Split the string back into lines and slice each line individually:

```python
lines = newString.split("\n")
slicedLines = [line[2:-2] for line in lines]
slicedString = "\n".join(slicedLines)
```
This slices each record (e.g. stripping wrapping characters like `{'` / `'}`) individually instead of the concatenated blob. If your real goal is just to strip quotes/braces from the list of URLs, skip the string round-trip entirely and slice the original list elements directly: `[item[2:-2] for item in myList]`.

You've mocked the entire `pyspark.sql` module, so `spark.createDataFrame(df)` returns a `MagicMock`, and calling `.count()` on it returns another `MagicMock`, not an int — `MagicMock` auto-generates attributes and return values but doesn't know `count()` should be numeric. Comparing that `MagicMock` to `0` with `>` fails because `MagicMock` doesn't implement `__gt__` against `int` unless configured.

Fix by explicitly setting the mocked chain's return value:

```python
mock_spark_df = MagicMock()
mock_spark_df.count.return_value = 2
spark.createDataFrame.return_value = mock_spark_df
```
or directly in the test:
```python
spark_df = spark.createDataFrame(df)
spark_df.count = MagicMock(return_value=2)
process_batch(spark_df, "123")
```
Either way, `.count()` must return a real `int` for `if data_frame.count() > 0:` to evaluate correctly instead of raising `TypeError`.

Handlers attached in `main.py` live on the logger named `'spam_application'` only; when you run `python -m my_pckg.foo`, that module's logger (typically `logging.getLogger(__name__)`) is a *different* logger object, and it only inherits your formatting if it's a child of the logger you configured — propagation follows the dotted-name hierarchy, not which file happens to run first.

Fixes:
1. Use `logging.getLogger(__name__)` consistently in every module, so `foo.py` inside `my_pckg` gets logger name `'my_pckg.foo'`.
2. Configure handlers/level/formatter once on the top-level package logger, e.g. `logging.getLogger('my_pckg')`, not on an unrelated name like `'spam_application'`. Child loggers propagate up to it automatically.
3. Put that one-time setup in `my_pckg/__init__.py` or a dedicated `logging_config.py` imported first (e.g. via `logging.config.dictConfig(...)`), so it always runs regardless of entry point, `-m` or direct script.

This is the classic map-matching problem, best solved with a Hidden Markov Model (Newson & Krumm, 2009): each GPS point is an observation, candidate positions along the known route are hidden states, emission probability is Gaussian in GPS-to-candidate distance (matching your ~5-10m error), and transition probability penalizes the ratio between route-distance and great-circle distance between consecutive candidates — enforcing realistic speed and forward order via a Viterbi decode over time-ordered states.

Don't hand-roll this; use an existing implementation:
- `leuven-mapmatching` (pure Python, HMM-based, good fit since you have one known route/graph rather than a full road network)
- OSRM's `/match` HTTP service or Valhalla's Meili map-matching
- `fmm` (fast map matching, Python bindings) for larger-scale offline batches

Since it's a single known route, build it as a graph and feed `leuven-mapmatching` your timestamped points, tuning its max-speed and GPS-noise-std parameters to your ~5-10m error.

Chroma changed the `EmbeddingFunction` protocol: chromadb ≥0.4.16 requires `__call__(self, input: Documents) -> Embeddings` with that exact signature, and rejects embedding wrappers still written against the old `*args, **kwargs` style — which is what your LangChain `SentenceTransformerEmbeddings` wrapper does under an older `langchain`/`langchain_community` version.

Two fixes:
1. Upgrade `langchain-community`/`langchain-chroma` to a version whose embedding wrappers implement the new signature — the actively maintained path.
2. Or pin `chromadb<0.4.16` in requirements to keep the interface your current LangChain version expects.

Alternatively, bypass LangChain's wrapper and use chromadb's own utility, which already matches the new interface:
```python
from chromadb.utils import embedding_functions
embedding_function = embedding_functions.SentenceTransformerEmbeddingFunction(model_name="all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
```
and pass that directly to `Chroma.from_documents`.

This is expected and harmless — PyCharm flags `instance._age` because, from plain static analysis, `Age.__get__`/`__set__` access an underscore-prefixed ("protected") attribute on `Employee`, a different class than `Age`. PyCharm doesn't specially reason about the descriptor protocol, so it can't tell this cross-class access is exactly how descriptors are meant to work.

Your code is correct; nothing to fix functionally. Options:
- Suppress locally: `# noinspection PyProtectedMember` above the line.
- Disable the inspection in Settings → Editor → Inspections.
- Avoid touching `instance.__dict__` under a name at all by storing data inside the descriptor itself, e.g. a `WeakKeyDictionary` keyed by instance:
```python
from weakref import WeakKeyDictionary

class Age:
    def __init__(self):
        self.data = WeakKeyDictionary()
    def __set__(self, instance, value):
        if value > 200:
            raise ValueError("Age cannot be more than 200")
        self.data[instance] = value
    def __get__(self, instance, owner):
        return self if instance is None else self.data[instance]
```

`scipy.optimize.minimize` has no combined `(f, grad, hess)` return convention the way `jac=True` covers `(f, grad)` — `hess` must be a separate callable. To still avoid recomputing shared terms, cache the last result keyed by `x` and have `hess` reuse it:

```python
import numpy as np
from scipy.optimize import minimize

_cache = {}

def obj_and_grad(x):
    key = x.tobytes()
    obj = np.exp(x) * x**2
    grad = obj + 2*np.exp(x)*x
    hess = obj + 4*np.exp(x)*x + 2*np.exp(x)
    _cache[key] = hess
    return obj.sum(), grad

def hess(x):
    key = x.tobytes()
    if key not in _cache:
        obj_and_grad(x)
    return np.diag(np.atleast_1d(_cache[key]))

res = minimize(obj_and_grad, x0=[1.0], jac=True, hess=hess, method='trust-exact')
```
Most trust-region methods call `jac=True` `fun` then `hess` with the same `x`, so the cache hits; clear it between independent optimizer runs if memory matters.

This is a CSS layout question more than a Django one — each button belongs to its own `
`, and `` is block-level by default, which is why they stack on separate lines regardless of how the views/URLs are wired. Keep the forms and views as-is and just change how they're displayed: ```html
{% csrf_token %}
{% csrf_token %}
{% csrf_token %}
``` ```css .d-flex form { display: inline-block; margin: 0; } ``` You're already using Bootstrap, so `d-flex gap-2` on the wrapper is enough on its own. Each form still posts independently to its own view, so your existing save/complete/delete logic doesn't change — only the wrapping markup/CSS does. Don't try to merge them into one `
`; that's what broke it when ChatGPT's fix combined the buttons.

`input()` returns the literal characters the user typed, including the two characters `\` and `x` — it never interprets escape sequences the way a Python string literal written in source code does. So `user_input_abc` is the 12-character string `\x41\x42\x43`, not the 3-character string `ABC`.

To interpret those escapes after the fact, decode with the `unicode_escape` codec, then re-encode to bytes:

```python
user_input_abc = input('enter user input in bytes: ')
decoded = user_input_abc.encode().decode('unicode_escape').encode('latin-1')
print(decoded)  # b'ABC'
```
`unicode_escape` interprets `\xNN` (and `\n`, `\t`, etc.) the same way Python's source parser does; re-encoding to `latin-1` maps the resulting code points 1:1 back to raw bytes. Avoid `eval()` for this even though it "works" — it executes arbitrary code from untrusted input, whereas `unicode_escape` decoding is the safe, standard way to turn escape-sequence text into real bytes.
